top.headline: A Republican Congressman Files Impeachment Articles Against His Own Defense Secretary
top.blurb: Rep. Thomas Massie filed eight impeachment articles against Pete Hegseth, citing Caribbean 'drug boat' strikes that have killed at least 221 people and a strike on an Iranian school that killed or injured more than 200 civilians. At his first Pentagon briefing in six months, Hegseth called the push 'sabotage' and insisted every strike was lawful, even as UN investigators have called the boat strikes possible crimes against humanity.

top.headline: Bill Gates Has Quietly Profited for Decades From One of America's Dirtiest Landfill Operators
top.blurb: ProPublica finds Gates holds 38% of Republic Services, the country's second-largest landfill operator and worth $29 billion — over a fifth of his net worth — while EPA inspectors have found more than 1,400 leak points at Republic sites since 2020, some venting methane at up to 300 times the federal limit. Gates, a prominent climate funder, has never publicly pushed the company to clean up, and declined to comment.

top.headline: A 'Gas Project' Near Alaska's Pipeline May Really Be Russian Intelligence Mapping the Arctic
top.blurb: ProPublica reports that Polar Train LNG, nominally based in Abu Dhabi, was steered by sanctioned Russian gas giant Novatek, whose surveyors mapped the Alaskan seabed near the Trans-Alaska Pipeline and an Air Force radar site through 2025 and 2026. The project's own CEO resigned in September alleging Novatek control, after which Trump waived sanctions-law requirements that would have blocked it.

top.headline: Two Adivasi Hamlets Are Missing From the Paperwork of Adani's ₹30,000-Crore Bihar Power Plant
top.blurb: Around 50-60 households in Pahariya Tola and Santhali Tola, inside the footprint of Adani Power's 2,400MW Pirpainti plant in Bhagalpur, don't appear anywhere in the project's environmental or rehabilitation paperwork, which states 'No R&R is involved.' Most residents are landless Santhal and Pahariya farmhands without title documents, leaving them fighting for recognition as project-affected people with no formal claim to compensation.

top.headline: An Adivasi Activist Dies Live on Facebook Accusing Officials of Harassment — Jharkhand Orders a CBI Probe
top.blurb: Nisha Bhagat, 39, died shortly after a Facebook livestream accusing Jharkhand's JMM government and land brokers of harassing her; Chief Minister Hemant Soren ordered a CBI probe after her parents alleged a conspiracy, and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes took suo motu notice. Bhagat had opposed the religious conversion of Adivasis and had voiced disappointment that the BJP and RSS hadn't backed her.

top.headline: A PAN Card and Voter ID Alone Can't Prove You're Indian, Gauhati High Court Rules
top.blurb: Ruling on a Foreigners Tribunal case, the court held that PAN cards and voter IDs are issued on self-declaration and can't establish citizenship unless the records behind them are proved too — upholding a ruling against Kulchan Begum, who could not establish her family's presence in India before the 1971 cutoff, and revoking her interim bail.

top.headline: Iran Denies Talks With Washington, Says the Strait of Hormuz Stays Shut
top.blurb: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei dismissed reports of US talks as 'a pure lie,' saying Tehran is still waiting on a response to seven conditions, including lifting sanctions and the naval blockade. Iran's Revolutionary Guards say three tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz this month, part of at least 37 attacks on shipping there — the highest monthly total since the war began — even as Washington says it remains 'open to diplomacy.'

top.headline: Russia and Ukraine Trade Strikes on Energy Grids as Baltic States Scramble Jets Over Drones
top.blurb: Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Ust-Luga export terminal and the Kirishi refinery, while Russian strikes cut power across Kryvyi Rih, Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia; Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia all issued drone alerts and scrambled NATO jets. The exchange came as US-mediated peace talks entered their final day in Abu Dhabi, with Zelenskyy calling the first day 'constructive.'

top.headline: US Charges Three Men Over an Alleged Iranian-Backed Plot to Attack a UK Air Base
top.blurb: US prosecutors charged three men tied to Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Iraq's Kataib Hezbollah over a plot to drive fuel-laden, shrapnel-rigged vans into RAF Fairford, the UK base used to stage B-1 bombers against Iran. The charges sit inside a wider indictment covering nearly 20 attacks across the US and Europe, including synagogue arsons and the stabbing of two Jewish men in London; Iran denies involvement.

top.headline: Afghanistan's Rahmat Shah Becomes the First Afghan Ever Ranked in an ICC Test Top 10
top.blurb: Afghanistan captain Rahmat Shah became the first Afghan ever ranked in the top 10 of any ICC Test category, rising six spots to 7th among batters after his 173 against Zimbabwe. The rise took him past Shubman Gill, Aiden Markram and Kamindu Mendis, a landmark for a team still finding its footing in the format.

top.headline: New Zealand Name Tom Latham's Test Squad for a First Meeting With India Since the 2024 Sweep
top.blurb: Tom Latham will captain a 14-player New Zealand squad for two Tests against India, starting November 19 in Wellington, with Tom Blundell, Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra all included despite injury concerns. It's the sides' first Test meeting since New Zealand's 3-0 sweep of India in 2024, with both teams still chasing a World Test Championship final berth.

bengal.headline: Presidency University's Expulsion Row Escalates — the Vice-Chancellor's Own Son Joins the Protest
bengal.blurb: Vice-Chancellor Nirmalya Narayan Chakraborty's son joined a protest against the expulsion of two Presidency students over an anti-ABVP poster, as alumni demanded reversal and ABVP pushed for legal action.

bengal.headline: Bishnupur Gharana Loses Its Last Great Sitar Voice, Pandit Manilal Nag, at 87
bengal.blurb: The Padma Shri sitarist, born in Bankura in 1939 and trained by his father, died in Kolkata, mourned as the man who carried Bengal's Dhrupad-rooted Bishnupur tradition onto the world stage.

travel.headline: A Seven-Year Camera-Trap Study Finds Threatened Wildlife Sheltering in Cambodia's Mangroves
travel.blurb: A seven-year camera-trap study across 156 sites in Cambodia's mangrove forests found fishing cats, hairy-nosed otters and critically endangered Sunda pangolins sheltering there, with some species tolerating life surprisingly close to villages.

happy.headline: A Vanished Bank Vice-President, an Amnesia Claim, and a Christmas Reunion His Sister Barely Recognized
happy.blurb: Letters found in a Key West attic in 1975 trace EM Martin, a bank vice-president who vanished in 1915 after frantically borrowing from Peter to pay Paul to keep Island City National Bank afloat; the Secret Service hunted him for two years until he surfaced in Australia, then returned to Oklahoma under a new name, claiming amnesia, and was only identified when a cousin spotted his photo in the paper — leading to a Christmas reunion with a sister he didn't recognize.

tech_top.headline: Anthropic Prices Its IPO at Up to $1.4 Trillion — Short of Its Old $2 Trillion Target
tech_top.blurb: Anthropic set a $70-$78 price range for its Nasdaq debut under the ticker 'ANT,' implying up to $1.404 trillion fully diluted — below the roughly $2 trillion it once targeted, but above its $965 billion valuation in May. The filing shows $81 billion in run-rate revenue against a $104 billion nine-month net loss, with Google and Nvidia each committing $10 billion; trading is expected to begin around November 19.
tech_top.pm_note: The dual-class structure — founders' voting shares, non-voting shares for public and strategic investors — means buyers of the $64B offering get almost no governance say, a template worth understanding before judging any 'public' AI company's real accountability.

tech_top.headline: Regulators Clear the First Small Nuclear Reactors at a US Industrial Site — but Not Until the 2030s
tech_top.blurb: The NRC approved a construction permit for four of X-energy's Xe-100 small modular reactors at a Dow chemical plant in Texas, the first such approval at a US industrial site, though the reactors won't run until the early 2030s. Amazon led X-energy's last funding round and has committed to buying 5 gigawatts of its capacity, as hyperscalers race to lock up nuclear power for data centers.
tech_top.pm_note: A reactor approved today doesn't generate a watt until the early 2030s — any roadmap betting that 'AI power constraints will ease soon' needs to price in that multi-year lag, not read the headline as supply arriving.

tech_top.headline: AI Companies Are Cracking Down on the Thing Hobbyists Loved Most About Them: Reverse-Engineering Hardware
tech_top.blurb: Hobbyists and security researchers say Claude and OpenAI's Codex are increasingly blocking or banning accounts used for reverse-engineering hardware — decompiling smart TVs, unbricking IoT devices — flagged as 'cyber abuse.' OpenAI says the blocks are mostly accidental; researchers say they're shifting to open-weight models like GLM 5.3 that carry no such restrictions.
tech_top.pm_note: Safety classifiers too blunt to tell 'hacking someone else's system' from 'modifying hardware you own' are pushing power users toward unrestricted open-weight competitors — a vivid case study in how trust-and-safety design choices shape competitive dynamics, not just risk.

tech_more.headline: OpenAI Acquires a Travel Startup From Sonder's Founder
tech_more.blurb: OpenAI acqui-hired Odessia, an AI travel-agent startup founded by Sonder's Francis Davidson, on undisclosed terms, as part of a travel push the company hasn't yet detailed.

tech_101.text: A nuclear reactor built far smaller than a traditional plant — 80 megawatts here — so it can sit at a single factory or data center instead of needing a dedicated utility-scale facility. None operate in the US yet; the earliest are years away.

A share structure where public investors get economic ownership but a separate class of founder-held shares keeps voting control — the structure behind Anthropic's IPO, where Class F shares carry 50.1% of the vote, leaving ordinary Class A buyers almost no governance say.

science.headline: Hubble Captures Visible-Light Proof of a Planetary Collision's Aftermath
science.blurb: University of Arizona astronomers used Hubble to photograph the 'Cat's Tail,' a 93-billion-mile dark dust structure around the young star Beta Pictoris, for the first time in visible light after JWST had only seen it in infrared. The team says it's likely debris from a collision between Pluto-sized bodies, and found Hubble also caught a separate warp in the star's dust halo, probably caused by a giant planet ten times Jupiter's mass.

science.headline: Purple Bacteria Turn CO2 and Industrial Waste Into a Billion-Dollar Supplement Ingredient
science.blurb: University of Valladolid researchers found purple phototrophic bacteria can produce coenzyme Q10, a popular energy supplement, and carotenoid pigments from CO2 and industrial waste gases instead of sugar feedstock. Their best strain, Rhodospirillum rubrum, hit CoQ10 yields approaching those of genetically engineered strains, though the authors stress this is lab-scale proof of concept, not yet commercial production.

science.headline: Fossil Fuel Emissions Are Set to Dip This Year, but Total CO2 Still Hits a Record
science.blurb: The Global Carbon Budget 2026, compiled by more than 140 scientists led by Exeter's Pierre Friedlingstein, projects fossil CO2 emissions will fall 0.4% this year, partly from an oil-demand shock tied to the Iran conflict, while deforestation pushes total emissions to a record 43.3 billion tons. Only about 150 billion tons remain in the 1.5°C budget — under four years at current rates — and researchers warn a geopolitically driven dip isn't a real peak.

philosophy.headline: Why Astrophysics Needs to Stop Treating Ordinary Matter as a 'Nuisance'
philosophy.blurb: Physicist Dylan Jow argues astrophysics unfairly treats real phenomena — dust, gas, ordinary matter — as nuisances obscuring the 'Big Questions' of dark energy and fundamental physics, a hierarchy he traces to Cold War-era physics funding rather than any inevitable truth. He argues the field should recover astronomy's older value as the study of real places and origins, not a cut-rate stand-in for a particle accelerator.

philosophy.headline: In Praise of the Dilettante, the Anti-Hero of an Over-Optimised Age
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Jay Miller defends the dilettante — the multi-interest amateur dismissed since Goethe and Schiller as a mere dabbler — as a legitimate way of life rooted in curiosity, blending Kierkegaard's rotating aesthete with Nietzsche's restless free spirit. He concedes the path forfeits recognition and mastery, but argues a specialization-obsessed age needs defenders of breadth over acclaim.

philosophy_101.text: Astrophysics' informal ranking of research priorities — dark energy and fundamental physics first, everything else treated as a 'nuisance' — which philosopher Dylan Jow argues is a product of 20th-century funding politics, not a fact about what's worth studying.

Originally Baroque Italian for someone who pursued an art purely for delight, the word curdled into an insult for shallow amateurism — philosopher Jay Miller argues it deserves rehabilitating as a deliberate alternative to specialization.
